theory.intro: A function of the form $(ax+b)^{n}$ is a power of a **linear bracket**. To find its primitive, add $1$ to the power, then divide by both the new power and the coefficient $a$.
facts: $\displaystyle\int(ax+b)^{n}\,dx=\dfrac{(ax+b)^{n+1}}{a(n+1)}+C$ for real $n\ne-1$ and $a\ne0$, on intervals where the real-valued integrand is defined.
The extra division by $a$ undoes the factor of $a$ that the chain rule produces.
Expansion is unnecessary for this rule. Expanding remains mathematically valid for nonnegative integer powers.
When $a$ is negative, $a(n+1)$ is negative if $n>-1$ and positive if $n<-1$. The sign of the primitive also depends on the bracket power and $C$.
A coefficient in front multiplies the whole primitive: $\displaystyle\int k(ax+b)^{n}\,dx=\dfrac{k(ax+b)^{n+1}}{a(n+1)}+C$.
The rule fails at $n=-1$, since $a(n+1)$ would be zero.
Check the answer by differentiating with the chain rule, which should return $(ax+b)^{n}$.
steps: Rewrite roots and bracket denominators as $(ax+b)^{n}$ with a single index
Add $1$ to the power to get $(ax+b)^{n+1}$
Divide by the new power $n+1$ and by the coefficient $a$

workedExamples.question_text: Find the general primitive of $f'(x)=(4x+3)^3$, then check your answer by differentiating.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Increase the power by $1$ and divide by the new power and the coefficient of $x$.
$\begin{align*}f(x)&=\frac{(4x+3)^4}{4(4)}+C\\&=\frac{(4x+3)^4}{16}+C\end{align*}$
Check using the chain rule:
$\begin{align*}\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{(4x+3)^4}{16}+C\right)&=\frac{4(4x+3)^3\times4}{16}\\&=(4x+3)^3\end{align*}$

Keep the multiplier $14$, then divide by the new power and the coefficient of $x$.
$\begin{align*}f(x)&=\frac{14(2x+5)^7}{2(7)}+C\\&=(2x+5)^7+C\end{align*}$

workedExamples.question_text: Find the general primitive of $f'(x)=\frac{8}{(5-2x)^3}$, writing your answer without a negative index.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Rewrite the denominator using a negative index.
$\begin{align*}f'(x)&=\frac{8}{(5-2x)^3}\\&=8(5-2x)^{-3}\end{align*}$
The new power is $-2$ and the coefficient of $x$ is $-2$.
$\begin{align*}f(x)&=\frac{8(5-2x)^{-2}}{(-2)(-2)}+C\\&=2(5-2x)^{-2}+C\\&=\frac{2}{(5-2x)^2}+C\end{align*}$

(a) Rewrite the square root using a fractional index.
$\begin{align*}f'(x)&=(2-5x)^{\frac12}\\f(x)&=\frac{(2-5x)^{\frac32}}{-5\left(\frac32\right)}+C\\&=-\frac{2(2-5x)^{\frac32}}{15}+C\end{align*}$
(b) A square root in the denominator gives an index of $-\frac12$.
$\begin{align*}g'(x)&=4(2x+3)^{-\frac12}\\g(x)&=\frac{4(2x+3)^{\frac12}}{2\left(\frac12\right)}+C\\&=4\sqrt{2x+3}+C\end{align*}$
(c) Rewrite the cube root using an index of $\frac23$.
$\begin{align*}h'(x)&=(3x+4)^{\frac23}\\h(x)&=\frac{(3x+4)^{\frac53}}{3\left(\frac53\right)}+C\\&=\frac{(3x+4)^{\frac53}}{5}+C\end{align*}$
